idiom_name: Ktor Sessions plugin with cookie transport and SessionTransportTransformerMessageAuthentication / SessionTransportTransformerEncrypt
implementation_notes: Ktor makes the client/server decision explicit: cookie<MySession>("name") passes the serialized payload to the client, while passing a SessionStorage keeps the payload on the server and sends only an id - the first form is this pattern. Protect the payload with a transformer: SessionTransportTransformerMessageAuthentication signs it (HmacSHA256 by default) so it cannot be modified, and SessionTransportTransformerEncrypt (AES plus HmacSHA256) also hides it from the client; cookie attributes (path, maxAgeInSeconds, extensions["SameSite"]) and the data class are configured in the same block. Custom headers are the documented alternative carrier for API clients that cannot hold cookies, which makes Ktor a rare case where the same pattern has both browser and machine-client transports out of the box.
pitfalls: Without a transform the session payload travels readable and forgeable; a sign-only transformer still lets the client read the content, so encryption is required for sensitive state.
The plugins' keys are byte arrays from configuration: rotating them invalidates live sessions unless a legacy transformer is kept for reads.
The session data class is serialized with kotlinx.serialization, so adding a required field breaks cookies already in flight - add defaults and version the payload.
sendOnlyIfModified is off by default, so the cookie is rewritten on every response, which costs bandwidth and creates lost-update races between tabs.
